text: Oliver Martin Johnston Jr. (October 31, 1912 – April 14, 2008) was an American motion picture animator and one of Disney's Nine Old Men, who was the last surviving member of the group at the time of his death from natural causes. He worked at Walt Disney Studios from 1934 to 1978, becoming a directing animator starting with the 1940 release of Pinocchio, and contributed to most Disney animated features, including Fantasia and Bambi. His last full work for Disney was on The Rescuers, in which he was caricatured as the cat Rufus, and his final film contribution was on The Fox and the Hound. He created or helped develop characters such as Mr. Smee (in Peter Pan), the Stepsisters (in Cinderella), the District Attorney (in The Adventures of Ichabod and Mr. Toad), and Prince John (in Robin Hood). According to the book The Disney Villain, co-authored by Johnston and Frank Thomas, they also created Ichabod Crane (in The Adventures of Ichabod and Mr. Toad), Sir Hiss (in Robin Hood), and Thomas served as a story consultant for Little Nemo: Adventures in Slumberland. Johnston and Thomas co-authored the reference book Disney Animation: The Illusion of Life, which outlined the 12 basic principles of animation and preserved studio techniques. Their partnership is featured in the documentary Frank and Ollie, produced by Thomas' son Theodore, who also produced Growing up with Nine Old Men, included in the Diamond Edition of the Peter Pan DVD. Born in Palo Alto, California, to Oliver, a Stanford professor, and Florence Johnston, he had two older sisters, Winifred and Florence. He attended Palo Alto High School and Stanford University, where he worked on the Stanford Chaparral with Frank Thomas, forming a lifelong friendship. He transferred to the Chouinard Art Institute in his senior year. Johnston married ink and paint artist Marie Worthey in 1943; she died on May 20, 2005, at age 87. In the 1980s and 1990s, he served on the advisory board of the National Student Film Institute and frequently presented at its annual film festival award ceremonies. Brad Bird paid tribute to Johnston with an animated cameo in the 2004 Pixar film The Incredibles and a cameo in his 1999 film The Iron Giant, where Johnston played a train engineer; both cameos included Frank Thomas. On November 10, 2005, Johnston received the National Medal of Arts, presented by President George W. Bush in an Oval Office ceremony. He died of natural causes on April 14, 2008, at age 95. Johnston's hobby was live steam trains; starting in 1949, he built a 4+3⁄4 in (121 mm) gauge La Cañada Valley Railroad with three 1:12-scale locomotives at his home in Flintridge, California, which his sons now own. This railroad inspired Walt Disney to build his own backyard railroad, the Carolwood Pacific Railroad, which later influenced the construction of the Disneyland railroad. Johnston was a founding Governor of the Carolwood Pacific Historical Society with fellow animator Ward Kimball. A 1:4-scale Victorian depot from his backyard was restored and relocated near Walt Disney's Carolwood Barn within the Los Angeles Live Steamers Railroad Museum in Griffith Park. In the 1960s, he acquired and restored a full-size, 3 ft (914 mm) narrow gauge Porter steam locomotive built in 1901, which he named the Marie E. He also built the Deer Lake Park & Julian Railroad (DLP&J) at his vacation estate in Julian, California, to operate the locomotive with a small gondola and caboose, using railroad ties from the defunct Viewliner Train of Tomorrow attraction in Disneyland. The DLP&J was 0.5 miles (0.80 km) long and first ran in 1968. Johnston sold the vacation estate and the narrow gauge train in 1993. The engine and its consist were later sold to John Lasseter (of Pixar Studios fame) around 2002. On May 10, 2005, the Marie E. ran on the Disneyland Railroad during a private early morning event organized by Lasseter to honor Johnston, who took the throttle one last time—this was the first time outside railroad equipment was permitted at any Disney Resort. The engine remains fully operational and currently runs on the Justi Creek Railway, located within the vineyards of Lasseter Family Winery, also owned by Lasseter.
